steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Roman family (familia) included everyone under the paterfamilias's authority — wife, children, slaves and dependants

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Patria potestas gave the father legal power over his children for life, even after they were adults

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Roman women could not vote or hold political office but managed households and could own and inherit property

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Marriage was typically arranged for political or economic reasons — the minimum age was 12 for girls

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: How much power did Roman women actually have? | Q: What was the difference between cum manu and sine manu marriage? | Q: How were Roman children raised?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Formally, women could not vote or hold office. However, they managed households, controlled domestic finances, could own and inherit property, and influential women like Livia shaped political events  | Cum manu: the wife passed into her husband's legal control. Sine manu: the wife remained under her father's authority, retaining her own property and family connections. Sine manu became more common o | Children received a bulla at birth for protection. Boys attended school or had private tutors; girls were educated at home. Infant mortality was high, and children from poor families went to work youn

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Balance formal legal restrictions with the informal influence women actually exercised Use specific named women as evidence: Livia, Cornelia, Clodia, the Vestal Virgins The contrast between legal theory and social reality is the key to understanding Roman women Roman epitaphs are valuable primary evidence for family emotions — use them Always consider class differences — elite women's experiences differed greatly from poor women's
